title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds: a global comparative meta-analysis
text:
Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
    A reproducible workflow for a global comparative meta-analysis
    
      
        Author
        Aneta Arct, Santiago Ortega, Agnieszka Gudowska, Karolina Skorb, Monika Gronowska, Magdalena Zagalska-Neubauer, Dorota Kotowska, Szymon M. Drobniak, Malgorzata Lagisz, Shinichi Nakagawa
      
      
        Published
        June 18, 2026
      
    
  
  
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
  




This book documents a reproducible comparative analysis of environmental variation and extra-pair paternity (EPP) in birds. The analysis uses population-level estimates of the proportion of sampled broods containing at least one extra-pair young and links them to environmental conditions, geography, species identity, phylogeny, and sampling structure.



The project is organised around three main environmental model groups: an environmental PCA model, a short-anomaly model, and a long-anomaly model. Each model group is fitted in two versions: a mean-only beta-binomial model and a location-scale beta-binomial model. All models include methodological controls for nest-box use and genetic marker type.




  Main question
  Do population-level EPP rates vary along broad environmental gradients related to temperature, precipitation, thermal variability, productivity, latitude, and distance to coast?

3.5 Basic variable cleaning

title: 3  Data preparation
text:
3.9 Reference-population overlap
The overlap between reference identity (id_reference) and population identity (population_id) is checked directly from the model-ready dataset. This summary was used to evaluate whether reference identity and population identity represented sufficiently distinct grouping structures. Because population identity captures repeated observations from the same species-locality combination, it was retained as the primary repeated-observation grouping factor in the full environmental models.


Show code
if (file.exists("data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds")) {
  overlap_dat <- readRDS("data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds")
} else if (file.exists("data/processed/dat_model.rds")) {
  overlap_dat <- readRDS("data/processed/dat_model.rds")
} else {
  overlap_dat <- read_csv("epp_data_June2026.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
    mutate(
      lat_round = round(as.numeric(lat), 2),
      long_round = round(as.numeric(long), 2),
      population_id = paste(scientific_name, lat_round, long_round, sep = "_")
    )
}

overlap_dat <- overlap_dat %>%
  mutate(
    id_reference = if ("id_reference" %in% names(.)) {
      as.character(id_reference)
    } else {
      as.character(id)
    }
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    population_id = as.character(population_id)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(id_reference), !is.na(population_id))

population_overlap <- overlap_dat %>%
  group_by(population_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_references = n_distinct(id_reference),
    id_references = paste(sort(unique(id_reference)), collapse = "; "),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

reference_overlap <- overlap_dat %>%
  group_by(id_reference) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_populations = n_distinct(population_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: 3  Data preparation
text:
3.10 Environmental window correlations
The main environmental models use environmental values from the first breeding-season month. As a data check, we compared these values with the corresponding full-season summaries for temperature, precipitation, diurnal temperature range, and NDVI. Because the correlations were high, subsequent analyses use the first-month environmental values and do not treat full-season summaries as a separate predictor set.


Show code
environment_window_pairs <- tribble(
  ~variable, ~first_month, ~full_season,
  "Temperature", "tmp_cru_C_first_month", "tmp_cru_C_full_season",
  "Precipitation", "pre_cru_mm_first_month", "pre_cru_mm_full_season",
  "DTR", "dtr_cru_C_first_month", "dtr_cru_C_full_season",
  "NDVI", "ndvi_first_month_median_30km", "ndvi_full_season_median_30km"
)

environment_window_correlations <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
  environment_window_pairs,
  function(variable, first_month, full_season) {
    keep <- complete.cases(dat_model[, c(first_month, full_season)])
    test <- cor.test(
      dat_model[[first_month]][keep],
      dat_model[[full_season]][keep],
      method = "pearson"
    )

    tibble(
      variable = variable,
      n_complete = sum(keep),
      pearson_r = unname(test$estimate),
      lower_95_ci = test$conf.int[1],
      upper_95_ci = test$conf.int[2]
    )
  }
)

environment_window_correlations %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable()

title: 4  Taxonomy and phylogeny
text:
4.1 Overview
This chapter prepares the taxonomic and phylogenetic structure used in the Bayesian comparative analyses. Starting from the cleaned modelling dataset created in the data-preparation chapter, species names are linked to a Clements-matched avian phylogeny, the tree is pruned to the retained species, and a phylogenetic correlation matrix is generated for use in brms.

title: 4  Taxonomy and phylogeny
text:
4.9 Prepare phylogenetic grouping variables
Two species-level grouping variables were retained for the Bayesian models:

species_phylo - species identity linked to the phylogenetic covariance matrix;
species_nonphylo - species identity modelled as an additional non-phylogenetic random effect.

Including both random effects allows the models to partition variation attributable to shared evolutionary history and species-specific variation not explained by phylogeny.


Show setup code
dat_model_phylo <- dat_model %>%
  mutate(
    species_phylo = Clements_name,
    species_nonphylo = Clements_name

It describes the beta-binomial response model, the population, species, and phylogenetic grouping terms used for the expected EPP probability, and the distinction between mean-only and location-scale models. title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.2 Response model
For record \(i\), the response is the number of sampled broods with EPP:
\[y_i = \texttt{n\_epp\_broods}_i,\]
out of the total number of sampled broods:
\[n_i = \texttt{n\_broods\_sampled}_i.\]
The model likelihood is:
\[y_i \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(n_i, \mu_i, \phi_i),\]
where \(\mu_i\) is the expected EPP probability and \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.3 Expected EPP and grouping structure
The baseline component for the expected EPP probability is:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta} +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The grouping terms correspond to population identity, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic species covariance:
\[u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{population}}),\]
\[v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{species}}),\]
\[w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{phylogeny}}\mathbf{A}),\]
where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the phylogenetic correlation matrix.
Here \(\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the model. The exact predictors differ between the environmental models, but the linear predictor always combines fixed effects with the same random-effect structure: population_id, species_nonphylo, and species_phylo with the phylogenetic covariance matrix.
In brms notation, this is:
(1 | population_id) +
(1 | species_nonphylo) +
(1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat))

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.4 Precision parameter
The parameter \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter. It controls the amount of residual variation around the expected EPP probability \(\mu_i\). Lower precision corresponds to stronger extra-binomial variation among records with the same expected EPP probability. Positive coefficients in the precision component indicate higher precision and lower residual overdispersion; negative coefficients indicate lower precision and higher residual overdispersion.
In mean-only models, the precision parameter is constant across records:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In mean-scale models, selected predictors are also included in the precision component:
\[\log(\phi_i) =
\gamma_0 +
\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}.\]
Here \(\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the scale model. Thus, mean-only models ask whether predictors explain average EPP, whereas mean-scale models additionally ask whether predictors explain variation in the precision of EPP estimates.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.5 Baseline overall model
The baseline overall model uses only the common grouping structure, without environmental predictors:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The precision component is:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In brms notation:

title: 6  PCA for environmental predictors

6.1 Overview
The environmental predictors combine climate, productivity, and geography. These variables describe related ecological gradients and should not be interpreted as fully independent axes of variation. title: 6  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
6.3 PCA construction
The sign of a PCA axis is arbitrary. PC1 is oriented so that higher values correspond to higher temperature loadings. PC2 is oriented so that higher values correspond to wetter and more productive environments.


Show code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

pca_source <- dat_model_phylo %>%
  mutate(
    pca_record_id = if ("epp_row_id" %in% names(.)) {
      as.character(epp_row_id)
    } else {
      as.character(row_number())
    }
  )

pca_raw <- pca_source %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_record_id,
    tmp = tmp_cru_C_first_month,
    pre_log = log1p(pre_cru_mm_first_month),
    dtr = dtr_cru_C_first_month,
    ndvi = ndvi_first_month_median_30km,
    abs_latitude = abs_latitude,
    distance_to_coast = distance_to_coast_km
  ) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na()

pca_input <- pca_raw %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_record_id,
    tmp_z = as.numeric(scale(tmp)),
    pre_log_z = as.numeric(scale(pre_log)),
    dtr_z = as.numeric(scale(dtr)),
    ndvi_z = as.numeric(scale(ndvi)),
    abs_latitude_z = as.numeric(scale(abs_latitude)),
    distance_to_coast_z = as.numeric(scale(distance_to_coast))
  )

pca_vars <- pca_input %>%
  select(-pca_record_id)

pca <- prcomp(pca_vars, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)

pc1_direction <- ifelse(pca$rotation["tmp_z", "PC1"] < 0, -1, 1)
pc2_direction <- ifelse(sum(pca$rotation[c("pre_log_z", "ndvi_z"), "PC2"]) < 0, -1, 1)

pca$x[, "PC1"] <- pc1_direction * pca$x[, "PC1"]
pca$rotation[, "PC1"] <- pc1_direction * pca$rotation[, "PC1"]
pca$x[, "PC2"] <- pc2_direction * pca$x[, "PC2"]
pca$rotation[, "PC2"] <- pc2_direction * pca$rotation[, "PC2"]

scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_input$pca_record_id,
    PC1_thermal_geographic = PC1,
    PC2_wet_productive = PC2
  )

  left_join(scores, by = "pca_record_id")

  inner_join(scores, by = "pca_record_id")

  "data/processed/dat_model_with_environment_geography_pca.rds"

6  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
6.7 Interpretation
Based on the loadings, PC1 was interpreted as a thermal-geographic gradient. In this dataset, higher PC1 values correspond to warmer sites with greater diurnal temperature range, lower absolute latitude, and greater distance from the coast.
Based on the loadings, PC2 was interpreted as a wet-productivity gradient after orienting the axis. In this dataset, higher PC2 values correspond to wetter sites with higher NDVI.
These two axes are used as the main environmental predictors in the beta-binomial EPP models.

title: 7  Main environmental models
7  Main environmental models
text:
The PCA models tested whether broad environmental-geographic gradients were associated with EPP.
The short-anomaly models tested whether recent deviations from local climatic conditions, measured over the five-year period preceding the breeding record, were associated with EPP.
The long-anomaly models tested whether deviations from the 1961-1989 climatic baseline were associated with EPP.

9.6 Location-scale model diagnostics
The location-scale models were fitted to evaluate whether environmental predictors and methodological controls also explained variation in the beta-binomial precision parameter. In brms::beta_binomial(link_phi = "log"), positive coefficients in the precision component indicate higher precision and lower residual overdispersion, whereas negative coefficients indicate lower precision and higher residual overdispersion.
The fitted location-scale models did not show sampler pathologies: no divergent transitions or maximum-treedepth hits were detected. However, the scale-component coefficients were generally estimated with wide credible intervals that overlapped zero. These results therefore provide limited support for interpreting predictor-specific changes in residual overdispersion, and the location-scale models are treated as exploratory rather than as the primary presentation set.

9.7 Predictive support for location-scale models
We planned to compare each location-scale model with its corresponding mean-only model using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation. In practice, these comparisons could not be completed consistently for the full environmental model set because LOO computation for the more complex location-scale models produced errors and/or unstable Pareto-k diagnostics.

This chapter collects figures used in the workflow. ## Sampling Locations
This map shows the geographic distribution of population-level EPP records included in the model-ready dataset. Point colour represents the observed proportion of broods containing at least one extra-pair young, while point size represents the number of sampled broods. This figure shows the phylogenetic distribution of species with the highest observed species-level EPP rates. Highlighted tips represent the species with the highest aggregate EPP estimates among species included in the pruned phylogeny. The figure is descriptive and is used to illustrate that high EPP values are distributed across the avian phylogeny rather than being restricted to a single narrow clade.
Show code
tree_file <- "data/processed/tree_pruned.rds"
dat_phylo_file <- "data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds"

if (file.exists(tree_file) &&
    file.exists(dat_phylo_file) &&
    requireNamespace("ape", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tree_pruned <- readRDS(tree_file)
  dat_phylo <- readRDS(dat_phylo_file)

  high_epp_species <- dat_phylo %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(species_phylo),
      !is.na(n_epp_broods),
      !is.na(n_broods_sampled),
      n_broods_sampled > 0
    ) %>%
    group_by(species_phylo) %>%
    summarise(
      n_records = n(),
      total_broods = sum(n_broods_sampled),
      total_epp_broods = sum(n_epp_broods),
      species_epp_rate = total_epp_broods / total_broods,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(species_phylo %in% tree_pruned$tip.label) %>%
    arrange(desc(species_epp_rate), desc(total_broods)) %>%
    slice_head(n = 10)

  write_csv(
    high_epp_species,
    "figures/high_epp_species_for_phylogeny.csv"
  )

  top_species <- high_epp_species$species_phylo
  tip_colours <- ifelse(tree_pruned$tip.label %in% top_species, plot_rust, "grey55")

  make_phylogeny_plot <- function() {
    ape::plot.phylo(
      tree_pruned,
      type = "fan",
      show.tip.label = FALSE,
      edge.color = "grey70",
      edge.width = 0.7,
      no.margin = TRUE

    ape::tiplabels(
      pch = 21,
      bg = tip_colours,
      col = "white",
      cex = ifelse(tree_pruned$tip.label %in% top_species, 1.1, 0.45),
      lwd = 0.25

    legend(
      "topleft",
      legend = c("Top species-level EPP", "Other species"),
      pt.bg = c(plot_rust, "grey55"),
      pch = 21,
      pt.cex = c(1.1, 0.7),
      bty = "n",
      cex = 0.85

    legend(
      "bottomleft",
      legend = gsub("_", " ", top_species),
      pch = 21,
      pt.bg = plot_rust,
      bty = "n",
      cex = 0.55,
      title = "Highest EPP species"

  dev.off()

  dev.off()

10.2 First Month vs Full Season
This figure compares environmental values extracted for the first breeding-season month with values extracted across the full breeding season. Stronger correspondence indicates that the first-month measure captures much of the same environmental variation as the full-season measure, whereas weaker correspondence suggests that the two temporal windows may capture different aspects of breeding-season conditions. This comparison supports the choice and interpretation of temporal windows used in the environmental models.

These figures summarise fixed-effect estimates from the three mean-only main environmental models.     mutate(

    "ndvi_first_month_median_30km_z", "NDVI"

    x_range <- range(dat_sensitivity_effects[[variable]], na.rm = TRUE)
    x_grid <- seq(x_range[1], x_range[2], length.out = 80)

    newdata <- dat_sensitivity_effects[rep(1, length(x_grid)), , drop = FALSE]

  fig_sensitivity_fixed_effects <- ggplot(

  ) +

    geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, y = predictor, yend = predictor), linewidth = 0.8, colour = plot_green) +

    plot_data <- main_fixed_effects %>%
      filter(.data$model == .env$model) %>%

      dpi = 300
    )

      file.path("figures", paste0(file_stem, ".pdf")),
      fig,
      width = 8,
      height = ifelse(nrow(plot_data) <= 6, 3.2, 3.8)
    )
  }

  pwalk(main_mean_models, make_main_mean_forest)

  ref_row$PC1_thermal_geographic <- 0
  ref_row$PC2_wet_productive <- 0
  ref_row$n_broods_sampled <- 1
  ref_row$n_epp_broods <- 0
  ref_row$nest_box <- factor("no", levels = levels(dat_main_pca$nest_box))
  ref_row$marker_type <- factor("DNA fingerprinting", levels = levels(dat_main_pca$marker_type))

  nest_newdata <- ref_row[rep(1, length(levels(dat_main_pca$nest_box))), , drop = FALSE]
  nest_newdata$nest_box <- factor(levels(dat_main_pca$nest_box), levels = levels(dat_main_pca$nest_box))

  marker_newdata$panel <- "Marker type"
  marker_newdata$level <- as.character(marker_newdata$marker_type)

  summarize_predictions <- function(newdata) {
    epred <- brms::posterior_epred(
      main_pca_mu_model,
      newdata = newdata,
      re_formula = NA
    )

    bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(ncol(epred)), function(i) {
      tibble(
        panel = newdata$panel[i],
        level = newdata$level[i],
        estimate = median(epred[, i]),
        lower = quantile(epred[, i], 0.025),
        upper = quantile(epred[, i], 0.975)
      )
    }))
  }

  main_pca_controls_plot_data <- bind_rows(
    summarize_predictions(nest_newdata),
    summarize_predictions(marker_newdata)

      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey90")
    )

  )

  ggsave(
    "figures/main_pca_controls_effects.pdf",
    fig_main_pca_controls,
    width = 8,
